content: Coconut milk is a sweet, milky white liquid that is extracted from the meat of mature coconuts. Its characteristic color and rich taste are due to its high oil content and natural sugars. In Malaysia, Brunei, and Indonesia, it is referred to as santan, while in the Philippines, it is called gata. It is important to note that coconut milk is distinct from coconut water, which is the naturally occurring liquid found inside a coconut. There are two main types of coconut milk: thick and thin. Thick coconut milk is made by directly squeezing grated coconut meat through a cheesecloth. The remaining coconut meat is then soaked in warm water and squeezed again, sometimes multiple times, to produce thin coconut milk. Thick coconut milk is primarily used in desserts and rich, dry sauces, while thin coconut milk is more suitable for soups and general cooking. In Western countries, this distinction is often not made because fresh coconut milk is rarely produced, and most consumers purchase canned coconut milk. Manufacturers of canned coconut milk typically combine both thick and thin extractions, often adding water as a filler. Depending on the brand and the age of the milk, a thicker, paste-like consistency may rise to the top of the can, which can be separated and used in recipes requiring coconut cream. Shaking the can before opening helps achieve a uniform, cream-like consistency. Once opened, canned coconut milk must be refrigerated and consumed within a few days, as it spoils easily at room temperature. Homemade coconut milk can be prepared by processing grated coconut with hot water or milk, which extracts the oils and aromatic compounds. It has a fat content of approximately 17%. When refrigerated, coconut cream naturally separates and rises to the top. Coconut milk is a staple ingredient in many tropical cuisines, particularly in Southeast Asia (including Filipino, Indonesian, Burmese, Cambodian, Malaysian, Singaporean, Sri Lankan, and Thai cuisines), as well as in West African, Caribbean, and Polynesian dishes. It is commonly found in the Asian food sections of supermarkets, either frozen or canned. Frozen coconut milk tends to retain its freshness longer, which is especially important in dishes where the coconut flavor is not competing with strong spices, such as curries. Coconut milk serves as the base for most Thai curries. To prepare curry sauces, the coconut milk is first cooked over high heat to break down the milk and cream, allowing the oil to separate. Curry paste, along with other seasonings, meats, vegetables, and garnishes, is then added. Coconut milk also has medicinal properties. The monolaurins found in coconut oil are known to possess potent antibacterial, antiviral, and antifungal properties. Additionally, some individuals believe that coconut milk can act as a natural laxative. Coconut milk is used in a variety of dishes across different cuisines. In Chinese cuisine, it is featured in various sweet dim sum dishes and sweet soups (tong sui). In Thai cuisine, it is a key ingredient in dishes such as red curry, green curry, massaman curry, tom kha gai, satay, sweet sticky rice, tapioca pudding, coconut pudding, and ice cream. Thai shaved ice, also known as Nam Kang Sai or Wan-Yen, is a popular cold dessert in Thailand. Unlike shaved ice in other countries, the Thai version places the toppings at the bottom, with the shaved ice on top. There are 20–30 varieties of toppings, including young coconut soaked in coconut milk, black sticky rice, chestnuts, sweetened taro, red beans, and chewy, slippery flour-based ingredients like cheng-sim-ee, among others.
